references.text: In [ref:5 Mos 20:10-11|Deuteronomy 20:10-11], the law is given to offer peace before going to war against a city. This is the background for the image Jesus uses of a king who sends a delegation of peace while the opponent is still far away.

In [ref:2 Sam 10:19|2 Samuel 10:19], the kings who were allies with Hadadezer make peace with Israel after realizing they could not stand against them. An example of seeking peace when one acknowledges their inferiority.

In [ref:1 Kong 20:18|1 Kings 20:18], Ben-Hadad sends a message, and Ahab responds – an image of diplomacy and negotiations for peace in a war situation, just as the king in Jesus' parable sends envoys to ask for terms of peace.

In [ref:Jes 27:5|Isaiah 27:5], there is an encouragement to take hold of God's protection and make peace with Him. The parable in Luke 14 points to settling accounts with God while there is still time, which aligns with Isaiah's image.

In [ref:Jes 36:16|Isaiah 36:16], the Assyrian king's envoy encourages making peace, with a promise of prosperity. The situation illustrates negotiating terms of peace when facing a superior power, as the king in the parable does.

[ref:Luk 14:28-31|Luke 14:28-31] is the immediate context: the parable of the tower builder and the king who goes to war, both about calculating the cost beforehand. Verse 32 concludes the parable of the king who realizes he is not strong enough.

In [ref:Luk 12:58|Luke 12:58], Jesus encourages settling with the opponent while still on the way. The same principle of seeking reconciliation in time, as the king sends a peace delegation while the enemy is still far away.

In [ref:Luk 14:33|Luke 14:33], Jesus gives the application of the parable: whoever does not give up all they own cannot be His disciple. Seeking peace with God involves total surrender, which is the point of the entire parable.
